summary: Defines a MIB module of textual conventions for representing common Internet network layer addresses, so other MIB modules can import them instead of defining their own.

eli5.summary: A shared way to write down addresses in network-monitoring lists so everyone writes them the same way.

questions: snmp textual conventions for ip addresses
how to represent ipv6 in a mib
what is a zone index in snmp
why not use ipaddress in a mib
subtitle: Shared SNMP MIB definitions for writing IPv4, IPv6 and DNS-name addresses, with zones, prefixes, ports and AS numbers.

tldr.problem: The SMIv2 IpAddress type holds only a 4-byte IPv4 address, which became a problem with IPv6, and MIB authors kept inventing their own address representations.
tldr.mechanism: A MIB module defines textual conventions: an InetAddressType value says how to interpret an accompanying InetAddress octet string, plus conventions for zones, prefix lengths, ports and AS numbers.
tldr.outcome: New MIB modules SHOULD use these conventions and SHOULD NOT use IpAddress. The RFC obsoletes RFC 3291.

today: RFC 4001 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3291. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why IpAddress Was Not Enough
sections.content:
Several standards-track MIB modules used the SMIv2 IpAddress base type, which can only contain 4-byte IPv4 addresses. That limited those modules to IPv4. RFC 4001 defines textual conventions (TCs) to express generic Internet network layer addresses in MIB modules, compatible with SMIv2 and SMIv1.

New MIB definitions that need network layer addresses SHOULD use these conventions, and new MIB modules SHOULD NOT use IpAddress anymore. Even modules that only need IPv4 or only IPv6 SHOULD use them.

The RFC says MIB modules that are IP version neutral should get new tables built on these conventions, with the old IP-version-specific tables marked "deprecated". Maintaining multiple similar tables for different IP versions is strongly discouraged. Generic transport addresses are not covered; RFC 3419 defines conventions for those.
sections.eli5: The old address box was only big enough for the short, old kind of address. This RFC gives everyone a roomier, flexible box.

sections.title: The Type and Address Pair
sections.content:
A generic Internet address is two objects: one of syntax InetAddressType and one of syntax InetAddress. The first value determines how the second is encoded. InetAddress is an opaque value, and InetAddressType "casts" it into a concrete convention. This makes the set of address types extensible.

A subnet is three objects: the type, the address and an InetAddressPrefixLength. A range of consecutive addresses is the type plus two InetAddress objects giving the start and end.

The two objects must stay consistent. Changing a type so that the dependent address would be undefined must produce an inconsistentValue error, so type and address change together. Compliance statements can require support for only a subset of the address types.
sections.eli5: It is like a label saying "phone number" or "street address" stuck on a box. The label tells you how to read what is inside.

sections.title: The Defined Textual Conventions
sections.content:
The module INET-ADDRESS-MIB (registered as mib-2 76) defines InetAddressType with the values unknown(0), ipv4(1), ipv6(2), ipv4z(3), ipv6z(4) and dns(16). InetAddress is an octet string of 0 to 255 bytes. Concrete forms are InetAddressIPv4 (4 octets), InetAddressIPv6 (16 octets), the zoned forms (8 and 20 octets) and InetAddressDNS (1 to 255 octets, fully qualified whenever possible).

The concrete forms SHOULD NOT be used directly in object definitions, since that restricts addresses to one format. InetAddressType itself SHOULD NOT be sub-typed in object definitions, but MAY be in compliance statements.

Other conventions: InetAddressPrefixLength (0 to 2040), InetPortNumber (0 to 65535), InetAutonomousSystemNumber, InetScopeType, InetZoneIndex and InetVersion.
sections.eli5: The RFC is a catalog of labeled boxes: one for each address kind, plus boxes for prefix length, port number and network number.

sections.title: Scopes, Zones and Prefix Lengths
sections.content:
A scope is a topological span within which an address is a unique identifier; a zone is one concrete connected region of a scope. Devices that connect several zones may hold identical addresses, so a zone index selects the interface. IPv6 link-local addresses are not guaranteed unique on a node, but an IPv6 address plus a zone index is unique.

The zone index is 4 bytes following the address. The value 0 refers to the default zone, which SHOULD NOT be used when the real zone index of a non-global address is known. For link-local addresses the index will typically be the interface index.

A prefix length of n means n contiguous 1-bits from the most significant bit. Values above the maximum are treated as the maximum: 32 for ipv4 and ipv4z, 128 for ipv6 and ipv6z, and 0 for dns.
sections.eli5: Two different houses on different streets can share a house number. The zone says which street you mean.

sections.title: Usage Hints for MIB Authors
sections.content:
Every use of InetAddress or InetAddressPrefixLength must say which InetAddressType object gives the context. It is suggested that the type object appear before the address in the conceptual row.

When an address is a table index, both objects MUST be used, with the type listed first, and the IMPLIED keyword MUST NOT be used. Instance sub-identifiers then look like T.N.O1.O2...On, where T is the type, N is the octet count and O1 to On are the octets. Because of the 128 sub-identifier limit in SMIv2, an index object MUST include a SIZE clause.

DNS names MUST be resolved when communication is needed, so object descriptions SHOULD say precisely how and when names are resolved. A host can have several addresses and names, so descriptions must say which is reported.
sections.eli5: When making a list, write down clearly which label belongs with which box, and how to look up names.

sections.title: A Table Indexing Example
sections.content:
The RFC's example is a peerTable listing communication peers by IPv4 address, IPv6 address or DNS name. It is indexed by peerAddressType and peerAddress. The address uses InetAddress (SIZE (1..64)), which forbids an empty address and limits DNS names to 64 characters to satisfy OID length constraints.

If a row is created by an SNMP operation with type dns(16), the agent stores the name and looks it up when contacting the peer. If the managed entity creates the row, it stores the IP address and does a reverse lookup when the value is read. A compliance statement restricts the type to ipv4(1) and ipv6(2) without zone indices.
sections.eli5: The example is a contact list where each person is listed by one of three kinds of address, with a rule about how long a name can be.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The module defines no management objects, only conventions for other modules to use. The RFC says meaningful security considerations can only be written in the MIB modules that define the objects, and so it has no impact on the security of the Internet.
sections.eli5: This RFC only gives out labels and does not run anything, so any safety rules belong to the lists that use them.

sections.title: Changes from Earlier Versions
sections.content:
Relative to RFC 3291, this version added a range restriction to InetAddressPrefixLength, new conventions InetZoneIndex, InetScopeType and InetVersion, explicit "d" display hints and updated boilerplate.

RFC 3291 relative to RFC 2851 added the prefix length, port number and AS number conventions, split the IPv6 convention into plain and zoned forms, introduced InetAddressIPv4z, and added the ipv4z(3) and ipv6z(4) values.
sections.eli5: The list of labels grew over three versions, with new boxes added each time.
